Before the first spoon

Build the flavor, then choose the form.

Dry jars

Use level measuring spoons. Here, 1 tbsp = 3 tsp and 1 cup = 16 tbsp; a teaspoon is about 5 mL. Powder density varies, so grams are not guessed from spoons. Whole seeds and ground powders are named separately.

The colored ribbon compares ingredient volumes only when every measure is compatible. It shows the measured proportions before mixing, not final yield or nutrition.

Fresh foundations

A dry jar cannot stand in for every tradition. Sofrito, mojo, kroeung, adobo and herb sauces also need fresh aromatics, liquids and cooking technique. Storage and starting doses appear with each entry.

Refrigerate fresh mixtures promptly at 4°C / 40°F or colder. Garlic and herbs in oil must be used within 4 days or frozen. A splash of acid does not certify shelf stability.

Taste with context

Start with a small amount in cooked food, then change one ingredient at a time. Cultural recipes vary by region, family and purpose; a pantry substitute is labeled as an adaptation.

Check allergens and ingredient labels, including sauces, sesame, mustard, nuts, soy and dairy. No recipe here is automatically kidney-safe, sodium-free, or a substitute for individualized dietary guidance.

Storage reference: Oregon State University Extension — herbs and vegetables in oil.

Your original question

Does that exact twelve-spice mixture have a name?

I have not verified an established name for that exact list. Onion, garlic, chili powder, cayenne, coriander, cumin, black pepper, turmeric, clove, paprika, ground mustard and ginger place it closest to a curry-style all-purpose house seasoning. That is a descriptive classification, not a confirmed traditional identity.

Your proportions were not supplied. “Andre’s Twelve” is a suggested starting recipe in this atlas, not a reconstruction of your actual mixture. In American shops, chili powder can already be a blend; a pure ground chile keeps the ingredient list at exactly twelve. Garam masala and za’atar are different flavor families.

The recipe below uses only your named twelve ingredients and clearly records the proposed amounts. Keep clove restrained and tune the heat after tasting cooked food.

    Make the idea yours

    A small, honest flavor lab.

    For a first trial, cook one small base portion and divide it into three tastes. Keep one unchanged; add a little acidity to the second and a little toasted or smoky aroma to the third. Write down exact measures, what food carried the seasoning, and what you actually tasted. A fantasy name describes a mood; it is never evidence that the blend tastes good.

    Restaurant names identify flavor inspiration. No proprietary formula, endorsement or affiliation is claimed. Flavor illusions aim for recognizable cues; they do not turn a food into another food or make it nutritionally equivalent.

    Sources link to the creators or official public flavor references consulted. The measured recipes and instructions here are original home formulations or transparent pantry interpretations, not claimed reproductions of those sources. Original experiments have no outside recipe source.

    Recipe references describe cooking traditions, not clinical approval. Nutrition has not been calculated. Ingredient brands, individual restrictions and portions matter.
